subject: Reproductive
vignette: A 19-year-old woman has had painful menstrual cramps since menarche. The pain begins just before or at the onset of menses and is accompanied by nausea; there is no abnormal vaginal discharge or fever. Pelvic examination is normal. She is told the pain results from uterine contractions that reduce blood flow and produce transient tissue ischemia.
question: Which of the following mediators is primarily responsible for the pain of primary dysmenorrhea?

options.text: Histamine
Prostaglandins
Bradykinin
Serotonin
Endothelin-1

explanation_correct: Primary dysmenorrhea is painful menses caused by increased uterine contractions that reduce blood flow to the myometrium, producing ischemic pain. It is mediated by prostaglandins released from the endometrium at menstruation. Because of this mechanism, NSAIDs, which inhibit prostaglandin synthesis, as well as acetaminophen and hormonal contraceptives, are effective treatments. It is distinguished from secondary dysmenorrhea, which has an identifiable structural cause.

explanation_incorrect.A: Histamine mediates allergic responses, not the cramping pain of primary dysmenorrhea.
explanation_incorrect.C: Bradykinin is a vasoactive pain peptide but is not the principal mediator of menstrual cramps.
explanation_incorrect.D: Serotonin is a neurotransmitter; it does not drive the prostaglandin-mediated myometrial contractions of dysmenorrhea.
explanation_incorrect.E: Endothelin-1 is a potent vasoconstrictor but is not the classic mediator targeted by dysmenorrhea therapy.

educationalObjective: Primary dysmenorrhea is prostaglandin-mediated ischemic pain from uterine contractions; NSAIDs are first-line therapy.

subject: Reproductive
vignette: A 22-year-old woman has an incidental 4-cm adnexal cyst found on pelvic ultrasound performed for a urinary tract infection. She is asymptomatic, with regular menses. The cyst is unilocular and simple. Hormonal evaluation shows mildly elevated estradiol. The cyst is thought to be functional/physiologic and expected to resolve spontaneously.
question: Which of the following best explains the formation of this cyst?

options.text: Failure of the corpus luteum to involute after ovulation
hCG overstimulation from a gestational trophoblastic tumor
Endometriotic implantation on the ovarian surface
Failure of a mature follicle to rupture and ovulate
Neoplastic proliferation of surface epithelial cells

explanation_correct: A follicular cyst is a functional (physiologic) cyst caused by failure of the mature follicle to rupture and ovulate. It is the most common ovarian mass in young females and may produce excess estrogen. Because it is functional, it usually resolves spontaneously. Other functional cysts include the corpus luteal cyst from failure of involution and the theca lutein cyst from hCG overstimulation; all may rupture, hemorrhage, or lead to adnexal torsion.

explanation_incorrect.A: Failure of the corpus luteum to involute produces a corpus luteal cyst with excess progesterone, not a follicular cyst.
explanation_incorrect.B: hCG overstimulation produces theca lutein cysts, which are often bilateral and associated with gestational trophoblastic disease.
explanation_incorrect.C: Endometriotic implants produce chocolate cysts (endometriomas), which are not simple functional ovarian follicles.
explanation_incorrect.E: Neoplastic surface epithelial proliferation would produce a cystadenoma, not a self-limited functional cyst.

educationalObjective: Follicular cysts result from failure of the mature follicle to ovulate, may cause excess estrogen, and typically resolve.

subject: Reproductive
vignette: A 27-year-old woman has a 3-cm simple ovarian cyst discovered on ultrasound. She is 3 weeks postovulation and has not been pregnant. Serum progesterone is elevated. The cyst is functional and is expected to resolve within a few menstrual cycles.
question: Which of the following mechanisms most likely produced this cyst?

options.text: Failure of the corpus luteum to involute after ovulation
Failure of the mature follicle to rupture
Excessive hCG stimulation of theca cells
Malignant transformation of a dermoid cyst
Obstruction of the fallopian tube with fluid accumulation

explanation_correct: A corpus luteal cyst is a functional cyst caused by failure of the corpus luteum to involute after ovulation. Because the corpus luteum secretes progesterone, this cyst may produce excess progesterone and can delay the menstrual period. Like follicular cysts, corpus luteal cysts are functional and usually resolve spontaneously, distinguishing them from neoplastic ovarian masses. Functional cysts as a group are usually asymptomatic but may rupture, become hemorrhagic, or cause torsion.

explanation_incorrect.B: Failure of the mature follicle to rupture produces a follicular cyst with excess estrogen, not a progesterone-producing cyst.
explanation_incorrect.C: Excessive hCG stimulation produces theca lutein cysts, which are often bilateral and linked to gestational trophoblastic disease.
explanation_incorrect.D: Malignant transformation of a dermoid is rare and would not present as a simple functional cyst.
explanation_incorrect.E: Tubal obstruction produces a hydrosalpinx, not an ovarian cyst.

educationalObjective: Corpus luteal cysts arise from failure of the corpus luteum to involute and may produce excess progesterone.

subject: Reproductive
vignette: A 28-year-old woman presents with abdominal distention and vaginal bleeding after a missed period. Ultrasound shows a uterine molar pregnancy and bilateral, multicystic adnexal masses. Serum hCG is markedly elevated. The adnexal cysts are functional and are expected to regress after treatment of the underlying gestational disorder.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis for these bilateral ovarian cysts?

options.text: Follicular cysts
Corpus luteal cysts
Mucinous cystadenomas
Endometriomas
Theca lutein cysts (hyperreactio luteinalis)

explanation_correct: Theca lutein cysts, also called hyperreactio luteinalis, are functional cysts caused by marked hCG overstimulation. They are typically bilateral and multiple and are associated with gestational trophoblastic disease such as hydatidiform mole or choriocarcinoma. Because they are functional, they regress once the hCG stimulus is removed. Bilateral multicystic ovaries in the setting of a molar pregnancy are a classic presentation.

explanation_incorrect.A: Follicular cysts are usually unilateral and single and are caused by failure of follicle rupture, not hCG overstimulation.
explanation_incorrect.B: Corpus luteal cysts are usually unilateral and result from failure of the corpus luteum to involute, not from high hCG.
explanation_incorrect.C: Mucinous cystadenomas are benign epithelial neoplasms that are multiloculated but not driven by hCG or associated with molar pregnancy.
explanation_incorrect.D: Endometriomas are chocolate cysts from endometriosis, not hormone-driven bilateral functional cysts.

educationalObjective: Bilateral theca lutein cysts reflect hCG overstimulation and are strongly associated with gestational trophoblastic disease.
